### Initial settings + load packages:
```{r message = F}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggridges)
library(patchwork)
library(p8105.datasets)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

options(
  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"
)

scale_colour_discrete = scale_color_viridis_d
scale_fill_discrete = scale_fill_viridis_d
```

# Problem 1

Loading dataset:
```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
```


Data cleaning:
```{r}
ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |> 
  mutate(month = lubridate::month(date), year = lubridate::year(date), day = lubridate::day(date),
         prcp = prcp/100, snow = snow/10, snwd = snwd/10, 
         tmax = as.numeric(tmax), tmin = as.numeric(tmin),
         tmax = tmax/10, tmin = tmin/10)
```

* Separate `date` variable into `month`, `day`, `year` variables
* Converting `prcp`, `snow`, and `snwd` into centimeters
* Converting `tmax` and `tmin` from character to numeric
* Converting `tmax` and `tmin` from tenth of degrees C into degrees C

This dataset has `r nrow(ny_noaa_df)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa_df)` variables once dates are parsed out into month, day, and year separately. It is describing precipitation and temperature across several weather stations and dates across `r nrow(distinct(ny_noaa_df, year))` years. There are `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa_df))` missing values across the whole dataset, which is quite a bit.


For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? 
```{r}
ny_noaa_df |> 
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |> 
  head()
```
The most commonly observed values are 0 cm (since most days of the year do not have snow), followed by missing values, then 2.5 cm.

Two-panel plot showing average max temperature in January and in July: 
```{r maxtemp}
ny_noaa_df |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |> 
  mutate(month = recode(month, `1` = "January", `7` = "July")) |> 
  group_by(id, month, year) |> 
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .25) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum temperature plot",
    x = "year",
    y = "Average max temperature (C)"
  )
```
The average maximum temperature is much higher in July (around 25-30 degrees C) compared to January (around -10 to 10 degrees C) across all years in our sample.

Two-panel plot showing the following:

* 1. tmax vs tmin for the full dataset:
* 2. distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year:
```{r twopanel}
tmax_tmin_p =
  ny_noaa_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmax, y = tmin)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum temperature",
    x = "Maximum temperature (C)",
    y = "Minimum temperature (C)"
  )

snow_p =
  ny_noaa_df |> 
  filter(0 < snow & snow < 100) |> 
  mutate(year = as.factor(year)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall density plots by year",
    x = "Snowfall (cm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

tmax_tmin_p + snow_p
```


# Problem 2

Read in datasets:
```{r read_accel}
demo_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4, na = c("","NA",".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(sex = recode(sex, 
                      `1` = "Male", 
                      `2` = "Female"),
         education = as.factor(recode(education, 
                                      `1` = "Less than high school", 
                                      `2` = "High school equivalent", 
                                      `3` = "More than high school"))) |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na()

accel_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv", na = c("","NA",".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

final_accel_df = 
  left_join(demo_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")
```

* include all originally observed variables
* exclude participants less than 21 years of age
* exclude those with missing demographic data
* encode data with reasonable variable classes: sex is now male and female, education is a factor variable with less than hs, hs equivalent, and more than hs as different categories

Producing a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category:
```{r educ_sex}
final_accel_df |> 
  group_by(sex, education) |> 
  summarize(n = n()) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

The majority of women have more than a high school degree at (n = 59). Similarly, the majority of men have more than a high school degree at (n = 56). 


Visualizing the distribution of age of men and women in each education category:
```{r age_educ}
final_accel_df |> 
  group_by(sex, education) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .3) +
  facet_grid (. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of age by sex at each education level",
    x = "Age (yrs)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

More younger women than younger men have more than a high school degree, though it approximately evens out as they age. The distribution of age for those with less than a high school degree is similar across sex. Fewer younger women have a high school equivalent degree compared to younger men. However, more older women have a high school equivalent degree compared to older men. 

```{r activity}
final_accel_df |> 
  mutate(total = rowSums(across(min1:min1440))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  facet_grid (. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total activity by age and sex, stratified by education level",
    x = "Age (yrs)",
    y = "Total activity in a day"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

As age increases, the total activity in a day generally decreases across all education levels. Additionally, the difference between men and women's total activity evens out at the oldest ages in our sample. For women with a high school equivalent degree, the peak activity occurs around 40 years of age. The demographic with the highest total activity in a day is women with less than a high school degree in their mid-20s. 

Three-panel plot showing the 24-hr activity time courses for each education level:
```{r activity_educ}
final_accel_df |> 
  pivot_longer(min1:min1440, names_to = "minute", names_prefix = "min", values_to = "activity") |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute), hour = minute/60) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = activity, color = sex)) +
  facet_grid (. ~ education) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth() +
  labs(
    title = "Activity over the day for each education level",
    x = "Hour of the day",
    y = "Activity"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Those with a higher education level have several outliers of peak activity level at a couple points in the day (around 8:00 am for women and around 8:00 pm for men) as opposed to the other education levels. However, across all education levels, activity is usually lowest in the beginning of the day until 5:00 am, where it increases dramatically and remains somewhat stable from 10:00 am to around 6:00 pm. The activity throughout the day is also very similar in shape for both men and women in each of the education levels.

# Problem 3

Reading in and combining files:
```{r read_bike}
jan_2020_df =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv", na = c("","NA",".")) |> 
  mutate(month = "Jan", year = 2020)

jan_2024_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv", na = c("","NA",".")) |> 
  mutate(month = "Jan", year = 2024)

jul_2020_df =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv", na = c("","NA",".")) |> 
  mutate(month = "Jul", year = 2020)

jul_2024_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv", na = c("","NA",".")) |> 
  mutate(month = "Jul", year = 2024)

all_df =
  bind_rows(jan_2020_df, jan_2024_df, jul_2020_df, jul_2024_df)
```

* all column names are already clean
* added in month and year to label observations before combining
* combined all observations into one dataset using `bind_rows`


Producing a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members:
```{r rides_time}
all_df |> 
  group_by(member_casual, month, year) |> 
  summarize(N = n()) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

The fewest rides for casual riders happened in January 2020 (n = 984), and the most rides for casual riders happened in July 2024 (n = 10894). In general, for casual riders, more rides happen in July and in 2024 than in January or in 2020. The fewest rides for Citi Bike members happened in January 2020 (n = 11436), and the most rides for casual riders happened in July 2024 (n = 36262). In general, for Citi Bike members, fewer rides happened in 2020 as opposed to 2024. 

Table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024:
```{r pop_station}
all_df |>
  filter(month == "Jul", year == 2024) |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarize(N = n()) |> 
  mutate(popularity_rank = min_rank(desc(N))) |> 
  arrange(popularity_rank) |> 
  slice_head(n = 5) |> 
  relocate(popularity_rank) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

The most popular station in July 2024 was Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers, with 163 rides originating from this station. The second most popular station was University Pl and E 14 St, followed by W 21 St and 6 Ave. The first five most popular starting stations all look to be in mid-to-lower Manhattan.

Plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration, swapping to default  color palette since yellow dots are not clear against the white background:
```{r duration}
jan_df =
  all_df |> 
    group_by(weekdays, month, year) |> 
    summarize(med_dur = median(duration)) |> 
    filter(month == "Jan")

jul_df =
  all_df |> 
    group_by(weekdays, month, year) |> 
    summarize(med_dur = median(duration)) |> 
    filter(month == "Jul")

ggplot(data = jan_df, aes(x = weekdays, y = med_dur, color = month)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = jul_df) +
  facet_grid (. ~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by day of the week, month, and year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_discrete()
```
People generally have a longer median ride duration on the weekends (Saturday and Sunday) compared to the weekdays. Additionally, The median ride duration is higher in July compared to January in both 2020 and 2024. The median ride duration for both months (January and July) in 2024 are lower than the respective median ride durations for both months in 2020. 

For data in 2024, figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration:
```{r duration2}
all_df |> 
  filter(year == 2024) |> 
  group_by(month, member_casual, rideable_type) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = duration, y = month, fill = member_casual)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ rideable_type) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of ride duration in 2024",
    x = "Ride duration",
    y = "Month"
  )
```
The distribution of ride duration in 2024 is right skewed overall, with several outliers in the higher duration ranges. The mean ride duration among members are usually lower than the mean ride duration among casual riders. The 75th percentile ride duration across all months, bike types, and members lie somewhere between 10 and 25 minutes. More outliers of extremely long ride durations happen during July compared to January, as well as with electric bikes compared to classic bikes.
